item.title: Ebola vaccine lessons | Science
item.description: Ebola occupies a unique place in popular imagination—universally feared for its high mortality and gruesome clinical presentations, it is often diagnosed only after it has been transmitted from patients to health care workers. The disease was first identified in 1976 at the Yambuku Mission Hospital in Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where 280 out of the reported 318 cases resulted in death, a harrowing 88% mortality rate. Six distinct strains of the virus that causes Ebola have been identified: Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo, Taï Forest (one documented human case), Reston (non-human primates only), and Bombali (bats only).

item.title: EDITOR’S NOTE on the Research Article “Mucus enhances gut homeostasis and oral tolerance by delivering immunoregulatory signals” | Science
item.description: On 25 October 2013, Science published the Research Article “Mucus enhances gut homeostasis and oral tolerance by delivering immunoregulatory signals” by Meimei Shan et al. (1). Comments on PubPeer (2) identified duplications within figure S20G and between figures S20B and s20G that were validated by Science and confirmed by the authors. The experimental work related to this paper was concluded in 2013, and the source data are no longer available. Science is posting this Editor’s Note to alert readers to these issues. We are not taking further action because the main conclusions of the paper remain supported.

item.title: US water protection maps undercount wetlands | Science
item.description: On 9 September 2026, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) proposed narrowing the definition of “waters of the United States,” limiting federal wetland protection to those touching perennial water. This criterion reduces eligible wetlands even further than the 2023 Sackett v. EPA standard did (1, 2). After the Sackett decision, 19 to 91% of nontidal wetlands were at risk of losing protection, depending on interpretation (3). The EPA’s own regulatory analysis could not produce a reliable national estimate and relied on qualitative judgment instead (4), in part because its National Wetlands Inventory (NWI), which was partially built from decades-old aerial photography, was not designed for regulatory use (4). Obtaining more-accurate and up-to-date wetland maps is therefore essential before revisiting the US rules that define protected waters.
